questions.question_text: Find the angle of inclination of $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix}$, to the nearest degree.

options.why: Used $\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y}$ instead of $\tan^{-1}\frac{|y|}{|x|}$, giving the angle from the $y$-axis.
Added $180^{\circ}$ to the reference angle even though the vector is already in the first quadrant.
Measured the angle clockwise from the positive $x$-axis instead of anticlockwise.

questions.solution_text:
Both components are positive, so the vector lies in the first quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{3}{8}$
$=20.56^{\circ}$
$\theta=A$
$\approx 21^{\circ}$

questions.question_text: Find the angle of inclination of $\underset{\sim}{b}=-5\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$, to the nearest degree.

options.why: Quoted the calculator's acute angle and did not use the quadrant.
Added the reference angle to $180^{\circ}$, the third-quadrant rule, instead of subtracting it.
Used the fourth-quadrant rule $360^{\circ}-A$ for a second-quadrant vector.

questions.solution_text:
Here $x<0$ and $y>0$, so the vector lies in the second quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}$
$=21.80^{\circ}$
$\theta=180^{\circ}-21.80^{\circ}$
$\approx 158^{\circ}$

questions.question_text: Find the exact angle of inclination of $\underset{\sim}{c}=\begin{pmatrix}-\sqrt{3}\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.

options.why: Quoted the calculator's acute angle and did not use the quadrant.
Used the second-quadrant rule $180^{\circ}-A$ for a third-quadrant vector.
Used the fourth-quadrant rule $360^{\circ}-A$ for a third-quadrant vector.

questions.solution_text:
Both components are negative, so the vector lies in the third quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
$=30^{\circ}$
$\theta=180^{\circ}+30^{\circ}$
$=210^{\circ}$

options.why: Gave the angle of inclination instead of converting it to a bearing.
Used the acute angle between the vector and north without checking which side of north it lies.
Turned anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise.

questions.solution_text:
Here $x>0$ and $y<0$, so the vector lies in the fourth quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{6}{6}$
$=45^{\circ}$
$\theta=360^{\circ}-45^{\circ}$
$=315^{\circ}$
$\text{bearing}=90^{\circ}-315^{\circ}$
$=-225^{\circ}$
$=-225^{\circ}+360^{\circ}$
$=135^{\circ}\text{T}$

questions.question_text: The vector $\underset{\sim}{w}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\12\end{pmatrix}$ is drawn with $\underset{\sim}{i}$ pointing east and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ pointing north. Find the direction of $\underset{\sim}{w}$ as a true bearing, to the nearest degree.

options.why: Gave the angle of inclination, measured from east, instead of the bearing measured from north.
Turned anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise.
Gave the bearing of the opposite direction by adding $180^{\circ}$.

questions.solution_text:
Both components are positive, so the vector lies in the first quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{12}{5}$
$=67.38^{\circ}$
$\theta=67.38^{\circ}$
$\text{bearing}=90^{\circ}-67.38^{\circ}$
$\approx 023^{\circ}\text{T}$

questions.question_text: Given $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-9\end{pmatrix}$, find the angle of inclination of $\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}$, to the nearest degree.

options.why: Quoted the calculator's acute angle and did not use the quadrant.
Used the second-quadrant rule $180^{\circ}-A$ for a third-quadrant vector.
Used the fourth-quadrant rule $360^{\circ}-A$ for a third-quadrant vector.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}1+(-4)\\2+(-9)\end{pmatrix}$
$=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-7\end{pmatrix}$
Both components are negative, so the vector lies in the third quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{7}{3}$
$=66.80^{\circ}$
$\theta=180^{\circ}+66.80^{\circ}$
$\approx 247^{\circ}$

questions.question_text: The vector $\underset{\sim}{w}=-9\underset{\sim}{i}+h\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ has an angle of inclination of $150^{\circ}$. Find the exact value of $h$.

options.why: Kept the negative sign of $\tan 150^{\circ}$ after dividing by the negative $x$-component, giving a third-quadrant vector.
Multiplied by $\sqrt{3}$ instead of dividing, using $\tan 60^{\circ}$ in place of $\tan 30^{\circ}$.
Multiplied by $\sqrt{3}$ instead of dividing and also kept the negative sign.

questions.question_text: A glider's velocity is $\underset{\sim}{v}=-15\underset{\sim}{i}-8\underset{\sim}{j}$, measured in kilometres per hour, with $\underset{\sim}{i}$ east and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ north. On what true bearing is the glider flying, to the nearest degree?

options.why: Used $\tan^{-1}\frac{|x|}{|y|}$ for the reference angle, swapping the two components.
Put the calculator's acute angle straight into $90^{\circ}-\theta$ without using the quadrant.
Turned anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise.

questions.solution_text:
Both components are negative, so the velocity lies in the third quadrant.
$A=\tan^{-1}\frac{8}{15}$
$=28.07^{\circ}$
$\theta=180^{\circ}+28.07^{\circ}$
$=208.07^{\circ}$
$\text{bearing}=90^{\circ}-208.07^{\circ}$
$=-118.07^{\circ}$
$=-118.07^{\circ}+360^{\circ}$
$\approx 242^{\circ}\text{T}$
